idiom_name: abstract Component class + List<Component> children (System.Linq.Expressions as the BCL instance)
implementation_notes: C# offers no language-level composite, so the structure is hand-written: an abstract class (or interface) Component declares the uniform operation, sealed leaf classes implement it, and a container class holds List<Component> and forwards the call to each child. Records plus pattern matching make closed node sets pleasant to consume, but the hierarchy itself is still yours to declare. The framework ships a domain composite worth reusing instead of rebuilding: System.Linq.Expressions.Expression is an immutable node tree whose operations are implemented by ExpressionVisitor, so query/expression problems should be modelled on it rather than on a hand-rolled mutable tree. Hand-write the classic hierarchy when nodes carry per-instance state and need reference semantics.
pitfalls: Expression trees are immutable: nodes cannot be edited in place, they are rebuilt through an ExpressionVisitor - treating them as a mutable composite silently produces a new tree that nobody keeps.
Child lists use reference equality for removal: removing a node needs ReferenceEquals semantics (or records, whose equality is structural) - mixing the two loses nodes.
Nullable reference types flag legitimately empty sub-trees; decide once between null children and empty collections, and validate on Add.
